Report Structures

You use that- clauses and wh- clauses to report statements and questions in indirect speech.
You use infinitive clauses and -ing forms to report statements, orders or questions in indirect speech.
You can use the Passive form to report events or situation in an impersonal way.
You use verbs like suggest, learn, report, say, believe or rumor in the Passive form to write or talk about impersonal reports.

You use reported speech to report statements or situations.
You use that- clauses to report someone else's thoughts or statements.

Example:
Jo suggested that I should go exercise more.

You use wh- clauses to report questions with wh- words like why, when, what, who, etc.
With wh- clauses, you normally use verbs like ask, want to know, wonder to introduce the clause.

Example:
Jo asked me when I was going to exercise next.

You use reported speech to report statements or situations.
You can use infinitive clauses to report someone else's thoughts or statements.

Example:
He promised to come with us the next time.
She strongly advised me not to miss the next seminar.
You use -ing forms to report actions. You sometimes need a preposition with some verbs.

Example:
He apologized for missing the seminar.
He recalled/remembered writing the event down in his agenda.

You can use the Passive form to report events in an impersonal way. The subject is not specific, but general.
You can use verbs like suggest, learn, report, say, believe or rumor in the Passive form to write or talk about impersonal reports.

Structure:

It+ Passive form + that ...
Example:
It is reported that too much overtime may be bad for your health.

Subject + Passive form + to ...
Example:
He is known to be a very understanding manager.
It has been reported on numerous occasions that repeated activities, no matter how apparently mundane, will eventually lead to injury
Most employees report having sought medical attention at one time or another.
Experts strongly advise workers find a release for their tension and stress.
It is said that meditation can help, and more and more employees have been embracing mindfulness.
The Reason Clause

You use reason clauses to express the reasons for an action, or why a situation is the way it is.
You use words like because, since, as, in case, and seeing that to introduce a reason clause.

Reason clauses are subordinate to the main clause. They state the reason why things are done, or what makes a situation the way it is.
You can use the following words to introduce a reason clause:

• because
You use because to explain the reason why something is the way it is.

• since/as
You use since or as to introduce a reason that is already known.

• (just) in case
You use in case to talk about things that may possibly happen.

• seeing that
You use seeing that to state that a situation is known.

You can use for, in that, insofar as, or inasmuch as to introduce a reason clause to give a reason for something.
For has a meaning similar to because.
Example:
We must begin planning, for the future may have some unexpected turns.

In that, insofar as, inasmuch as, have similar meaning. They are quite formal, and are commonly found in writing rather than in spoken English. The clause they introduce clarifies what has been said by adding more detail and information.
Example:
The film is unusual in that it only features 2 main actors.
You can use because of, due to or owing to to introduce a noun phrase that gives a reason for a situation.

Example:
She was injured because of an accident.
We have less money owing to / due to budget cuts.
You can use -ing clauses to express reason relationships between the main clause and the subordinate clause.

Example:
We queued for over two hours, hoping to get tickets to the seminar.
Having met the speaker personally, I can vouch for his enthusiasm.

images.text:
A Demanding Workload

Since the human body is frail, there seems to be no way to avoid the aches and pains associated with our daily workloads. It's been reported on numerous occasions that repetitive activities, no matter how apparently mundane, will eventually lead to injury. Seeing that modern humans work long hours, many end up with a wide range of ailments ranging from chronic neck problems to fatigue and tension. Most employees report having sought medical attention at one time or another.

Automation has already led to reduced workloads, and perhaps this will lead to healthier and longer lifespans. Maybe innovation in the way we do our jobs will allow us to live pain-free lives. We can't say for sure, though, because we don't know what the future holds. What we can do is focus on improving our current situation by paying attention to how we go about doing our jobs.

Experts strongly advise workers to find a release for their tension and stress. It is said that meditation can help, and more and more employees have been embracing mindfulness. Many employers have even suggested that employees attend mandatory meditation sessions.  A number of professions have also been encouraging an increased focus on posture. Slouching is a dangerous habit, since it puts a huge strain on the spine.

There's no shortage of solutions. Some professionals even see laughter and yawning as a way to reduce anxiety. If you've already tried everything, though, why not get a pet? It has been reported that owning a pet can vastly improve a person's well-being. Regardless, the first step to finding a solution is identifying that there is a problem. So if you've come to realize that your work may have a long-term affect on your health, you're already halfway there!
